```{r, include = FALSE}
# Figures are drawn on the REAL CPB canvas (page = "half" is 7.5 cm,
# "full" is 15.5 cm; text sizes in theme_cpb() are absolute points, so
# any other canvas distorts the text-to-figure proportion) and only
# *displayed* smaller via out.width, at a consistent 2:1 scale:
# half-page figures at 350px, full-page figures at 700px.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7.5 / 2.54,
  fig.height = 7.5 / 2.54,
  dpi = 300,
  out.width = "350px",
  dev = if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) "ragg_png" else "png"
)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(ggcpb)
```

```{r show-saved-helper, include = FALSE}
# Displays a file save_cpb() already wrote to a temporary path, at a
# stable location knitr manages itself -- so the rendered copy of this
# page (e.g. on GitHub) keeps a working image link rather than one
# pointing at a temp file that no longer exists. Purely a display
# detail for this page, not part of the save_cpb() example above it.
.show_saved <- function(path) {
  stable <- knitr::fig_path(".png")
  dir.create(dirname(stable), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  file.copy(path, stable, overwrite = TRUE)
  knitr::include_graphics(stable)
}
```

# Introduction

Most figures in this package are built by calling one of its
functions directly in R code. This vignette describes an alternative
based on CSV files. The datasets are CSV files in a folder named
`data`. One parameter file, `params.csv`, specifies which figures to
create and how they should be configured. The `cpb_import_csv()`
function reads them and creates the figures.

This approach is useful when figure specifications need to be kept
separate from R code, for example when the data and figure settings
are maintained outside an R script.

# The figure folder

A figure folder holds `params.csv` and a `data` folder. The function
`autogenerate_plots()` creates a ready to use example. It is used
throughout this vignette.

```{r kit, results = "hide"}
figure_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "figures")
autogenerate_plots(figure_dir)
params_csv <- file.path(figure_dir, "params.csv")
```

```{r kit-files}
list.files(figure_dir, recursive = TRUE)
```

In normal use, the folder lives somewhere you can write to, and the
start scripts (`run_import.bat` and `run_import.command`) run
everything for you. See "Run the import without opening R" below.

# The data files

Each dataset is a CSV file in the `data` folder. It can have any name
and holds the variables needed by the figures. The first row holds the
column names. The package example has two datasets.

```{r data-frame}
read.csv(file.path(figure_dir, "data", "koopkracht.csv"))
```

The important point for the import method is that the parameter file
refers to variables by their column names. For example, if a
parameter contains `jaar`, `cpb_import_csv()` looks for a column named
`jaar` in the dataset of that figure.

Text columns keep the order of the rows. The first group in the file is
the first on the axis and in the legend. A number used as `fill`,
`group` or `colour` (a year, for example) is treated as a category. A
numeric `colour` in a scatter plot keeps its colour gradient.

Save datasets from Excel as `CSV UTF-8 (comma delimited)`.

# The parameter file

The parameter file determines which figures are created. Each figure
has a `plot_type` and an `id`, together with the settings required
for that plot type. The parameter `data` names the dataset of the
figure.

The first column holds the parameter names. Every other column
describes one figure. This is the example file:

```{r params-raw, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
cat(readLines(params_csv), sep = "\n")
```

The same content, split on the comma and shown as a table:

```{r params-table, echo = FALSE}
params_df <- read.csv(params_csv, header = FALSE, fill = TRUE,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                      col.names = c("parameter", paste("figure", 1:2)))
params_df[is.na(params_df)] <- ""
knitr::kable(params_df)
```

A cell can be left blank. Fields at the end of a row can be left out.

The parameter `page` sets the page width a figure is saved at: `half`
(7.5 cm, the default), `full` (15.5 cm) or `small`. Leave it out for
`half`.

Some parameters refer to columns in the dataset. For example:

* `x`, `y`, `fill` and `sec_y` are column references.
* `title`, `ylab`, `position` and `data` are literal values.

The distinction is important. The cell next to `y` says `koopkracht`,
so the `y` variable is taken from the `koopkracht` column. The cell
next to `ylab` says `% mutatie`, so that text is used directly.

# Creating the figures

Pass the parameter file to `cpb_import_csv()`. The datasets are read
from the `data` folder next to it:

```{r build, results = "hide"}
figs <- cpb_import_csv(params_csv)
```

When the parameter file contains multiple figures, `cpb_import_csv()`
returns a named list. The names come from the datasets. Here the two
figures use different datasets, so they are called `koopkracht` and
`werkloosheid`.

The `koopkracht` figure has a second value axis (`sec_y`), and its
right side caption is only placed exactly by `save_cpb()`. Printed
directly, an approximate placement is shown instead, close but not
exact, since at that point the figure has not actually been saved yet
to measure against. So, rather than printing it directly, it is
written out through `save_cpb()` first and shown from that file:

```{r fig-koopkracht, results = "hide"}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
save_cpb(path, figs$koopkracht, page = "half")
```

```{r fig-koopkracht-show, echo = FALSE}
.show_saved(path)
```

`werkloosheid` has no second axis, so it can be shown directly:

```{r fig-werkloosheid}
figs$werkloosheid
```

# Several datasets

The parameter `data` names the dataset of a figure, relative to the
`data` folder next to `params.csv`. The extension `.csv` is optional,
so `koopkracht` and `koopkracht.csv` are the same dataset.

| `data` parameter | What happens |
|---|---|
| `koopkracht` | The figure uses `data/koopkracht.csv`. |
| `a;b` | One figure is made from each named dataset. |
| blank | The figure uses `data/data.csv`. |
| column absent | The same as blank. |

The figures are named after their dataset. If several figures use the
same dataset, the figure number is added to the name. The first figure
column in `params.csv` is number 1. For example, `koopkracht_1.png`
and `koopkracht_3.png`.

A named dataset that does not exist in the `data` folder is skipped
with a warning. Nothing
falls back to another dataset. The other datasets in the same list
and the other rows are still created. With `data` set to
`a;b;c` and no `b.csv`, you get figures for `a` and `c`, and a
warning about `b.csv`.

# A parameter file with one figure

A parameter file can describe a single figure. It then has one column
of values next to the parameter names. For example, the following
describes a line chart. It can be saved in the same folder, so it finds
the same `data` folder:

```{r one-figure}
params_one <- file.path(figure_dir, "params_one.csv")

writeLines(c(
  "plot_type,line",
  "title,Werkloosheid",
  "data,werkloosheid",
  "x,jaar",
  "y,werkloosheid",
  "ylab,%"
), params_one)

cat(readLines(params_one), sep = "\n")
```

When the parameter file describes one figure, `cpb_import_csv()` returns
that figure directly rather than a named list. Use `simplify = FALSE`
to always get a named list.

```{r one-figure-build, results = "hide"}
fig_one <- cpb_import_csv(params_one)
```

```{r one-figure-show, echo = FALSE}
fig_one
```

# Handling problems

A parameter can be left blank. In that case, the default value is
used.

If a parameter is not valid for the selected `plot_type`, it is
ignored and the default is used. These cases produce a warning.

If a figure cannot be created, for example because a column
referenced by a parameter does not exist in the dataset, that
figure is skipped. Other figures in the same parameter file are still
created.

Each call to `cpb_import_csv()` also writes a log file next to the
parameter file. The log records figures that were created or skipped
and any parameter problems.

# Run the import without opening R

The same CSV based method can also be used without opening R.

The `autogenerate_plots()` function creates a ready to use folder
containing:

* a `data` folder with the datasets
* a parameter file, `params.csv`
* a script for Windows (a `.bat` file)
* a script for a Mac (a `.command` file)

After editing the datasets and the parameter file, run the
appropriate script. It reads `params.csv`, builds every figure and
saves the images in the folder `generated`. Each image is named after
its dataset.

Running the script again produces updated figures. Images with the
same name are replaced. A dataset or figure that fails is skipped and
listed at the end, and in `params_log.txt`. The other figures are
still saved.

R and `ggcpb` must still be installed on the computer running the
script.

# Appendix A: Parameter values {-}

The available parameters depend on the `plot_type`. The complete list
is stored in `parameter_settings.csv`, and gives the available
parameters, their kind, default values and examples.

```{r params-ref-path}
ref_csv <- system.file(
  "extdata",
  "parameter_settings.csv",
  package = "ggcpb"
)
```

Many parameters are the same across every `plot_type`. To avoid
repeating those in every table, Table A1 lists the parameters shared,
with the same meaning and default, by all plot types. Table A2 onward
each cover one `plot_type`, listing only what is not already in Table
A1. A parameter is only listed for the plot types it actually applies
to, so a table for one `plot_type` does not necessarily match another.

```{r params-ref-table, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
ref <- read.csv(
  ref_csv,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

types <- unique(ref$plot_type)

# a parameter belongs in the shared table only when every plot_type
# has it, with the same kind and default -- present everywhere but
# with a different default per type (e.g. reverse_legend) still needs
# its own row in each type's own table, since a single shared default
# would be wrong for the types that do not use it
by_param <- split(ref, ref$param)
is_shared <- vapply(by_param, function(rows) {
  setequal(unique(rows$plot_type), types) &&
    nrow(unique(rows[c("kind", "default")])) == 1
}, logical(1))
shared_params <- sort(names(by_param)[is_shared])

show_params <- function(rows) {
  rows <- rows[order(rows$param), c("param", "kind", "default", "example")]
  print(knitr::kable(
    rows,
    row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = c("setting", "kind", "default", "example")
  ))
}

cat("\n\n**Table A1. Shared parameters across all plot types**\n\n")
show_params(ref[ref$param %in% shared_params & !duplicated(ref$param), ])

table_n <- 2
for (t in types) {
  rows <- ref[ref$plot_type == t & !ref$param %in% shared_params, ]
  if (!nrow(rows)) next
  cat("\n\n**Table A", table_n, ". Parameters specific to `", t, "`**\n\n",
      sep = "")
  show_params(rows)
  table_n <- table_n + 1
}
```

A parameter of kind `column` takes a column name from the data file.
A parameter of kind `literal` takes a value directly from the
parameter file.

The `parameter_settings.csv` file can also be opened directly in a
spreadsheet program.
